candidates.title: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats
candidates.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
candidates.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans.

candidates.title: LAMPS'26: ACM CCS Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Security Analysis
candidates.summary: The rapid transition from standalone large AI models to autonomous, tool-using agentic AI systems has reshaped the privacy and security landscape. Agents that plan over long horizons, invoke external APIs, and execute code open a system-level attack surface that empirical, patch-driven defenses cannot contain. LAMPS'26 emphasizes mathematically grounded protection, bridging agentic security with rigorous formal verification and advanced cryptography. The workshop examines agent-centric vulnerabilities such as skill exploitation, indirect prompt injection, unauthorized tool use, and multi-agent cascading failures, together with defenses that offer verifiable guarantees rather than best-effort

candidates.title: MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark

However, IPI benchmarks lag behind their rapidly evolving utility counterparts, only offering limited task and environment coverage and relying on narrow, static attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose meta-benchmarking for IPI: transforming existing utility benchmarks into end-to-end IPI evaluation suites that reuse their realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure. candidates.summary: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) poses a critical threat to LLM agents. Existing defenses largely focus on whether an injection induces a new tool invocation or unintended action. Such attacks are difficult to detect because no new action is introduced, while parameter changes themselves are often legitimate parts of the user's request. candidates.summary: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. candidates.summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces.
